[[Bill English]] | predecessor3 = [[Judith Collins]] | successor3 = [[Andrew Little (New Zealand politician)|Andrew Little]] | birth_name = Amy Juliet Milnes | birth_date = {{birth date and age|1971|05|19|df=y}} | birth_place = [[Auckland]], New Zealand | party = [[New Zealand National Party|National]] | spouse = Don Adams | children = 2 | profession = Lawyer | education = [[University of Canterbury]] | website = {{URL|http://amyadams.co.nz}} | order4 = 26th [[Minister for Social Housing]] | order = 16th Chancellor of the [[University of Canterbury]] | predecessor4 = [[Paula Bennett]] | successor4 = [[Phil Twyford]] | prime_minister4 = [[Bill English]] | term_start4 = 20 December 2016 | term_end4 = 26 October 2017 }} '''Amy Juliet Adams''' ({{nee|'''Milnes'''}}; born 19 May 1971) is a New Zealand lawyer and former politician. Since 2022, she has served as the chancellor of the [[University of Canterbury]]. Adams was a [[New Zealand National Party|National Party]] [[New Zealand Parliament|Member of Parliament]], representing the [[Selwyn (New Zealand electorate)|Selwyn]] electorate from 2008 to 2020, when she retired. She served as [[Ministry for the Environment (New Zealand)|Minister for the Environment]], [[Minister of Communications (New Zealand)|Minister of Communications]], and [[Minister of Justice (New Zealand)|Minister of Justice]] in the [[Fifth National Government of New Zealand|Fifth National Government]]. == Early life and family == Adams was born in 1971. When she was two, her mother divorced her father, raising her and her sister Belinda alone.{{cite news |last1=Wright |first1=Michael |title=Amy Adams on movies, mothering and money |work=[[The Press]] |date=11 October 2014 |page=A18}} Adams attended [[Rangitoto College]] on the North Shore of Auckland, where she was friends with [[Louise Upston]]{{cite news |last1=Vance |first1=Andrea |title=Amy not afraid to speak her mind |url= http://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/7323958/Amy-not-afraid-to-speak-her-mind |access-date=10 October 2014 |work=[[Sunday Star-Times]] |date=22 July 2012}} (also later a National Party politician), then graduated from the [[University of Canterbury]] with a [[Bachelor of Laws]] with [[First Class Honours|First-Class Honours]]. Her first employment as a lawyer was in [[Invercargill]], but she soon moved back to [[Canterbury, New Zealand|Canterbury]]. She became a partner in the [[Christchurch]] law firm Mortlock McCormack. Adams married Robert Donald "Don" Adams, with whom she has two children. The couple live in [[Aylesbury, New Zealand|Aylesbury]], close to the [[Fault (geology)|fault line]] and [[epicenter|epicentre]] of the [[2010 Canterbury earthquake]].{{Cite web|title=General Debate – 8th September, 2010 – Part 5 – YouTube|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BoysJBb4Ayo&feature=player_embedded |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211215/BoysJBb4Ayo |archive-date=2021-12-15 |url-status=live|access-date=2020-11-14|website=www.youtube.com| date=7 September 2010 }}{{cbignore}} They also own three farms in [[Darfield, New Zealand|Darfield]], [[Kirwee]], and [[Te Kauwhata]]. The first two of these are sheep and crop farms in [[Canterbury, New Zealand|Canterbury]], and within the area of the [[Central Plains Water]] scheme. Through their company Amdon Farms Ltd, the Adams family is a shareholder of Central Plains Water.{{cite news|last1=Strongman|first1=Susan|date=18 March 2014|title=Columnist stands by Amy Adams claims|work=[[Taranaki Daily News]]|url=http://www.stuff.co.nz/business/farming/agribusiness/9838125/Columnist-stands-by-Amy-Adams-claims|access-date=30 September 2014}} The Te Kauwhata farm is located in the [[Waikato]]. Adams' sister Belinda later worked in the office of [[Minister for Social Development (New Zealand)|Social Development Minister]] [[Paula Bennett]] and was appointed [[Superu|Families Commissioner]] in 2013.{{cite news|last1=Davison|first1=Isaac|date=20 July 2013|title=It's jobs for the mates – Labour slams Nats|work=[[The New Zealand Herald]]|url=http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=10900499|access-date=12 October 2014}} Adams' brother-in-law, David Ware is a telecommunications executive and publicly {{End}} ===Fifth National Government, 2008–2017=== Adams was selected as the National Party candidate for the Selwyn seat for the [[2008 New Zealand general election|2008 general election]] after a contested selection.{{cite news |author=Wilson, Peter |title=National selects Amy Adams for Selwyn Seat |url=http://www.nbr.co.nz/article/national-selects-amy-adams-selwyn-seat |work=National Business Review |agency=NZPA |date=12 May 2008 |access-date=26 December 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110611054326/http://www.nbr.co.nz/article/national-selects-amy-adams-selwyn-seat |archive-date=11 June 2011 |url-status=dead }} She won the seat with a comfortable majority, achieving 60% of the electorate votes cast. This compares with the National Party achieving 55% of party votes.{{cite web |url= http://www.parliament.nz/en-NZ/MPP/Electorates/EPData/0/1/d/DBHOH_Lib_EP_Selwyn_Data_3-Selwyn-Electoral-Profile.htm |title=Selwyn: Electoral Profile |publisher=New Zealand Parliament |access-date=10 December 2009}} In the {{NZ election link|2014}}, she won more than 70% of the electorate votes based on preliminary results.{{cite web |title=Election Results – Selwyn |url= http://electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2014/electorate-48.html |access-date=30 September 2014 |publisher=[[Electoral Commission (New Zealand)|Electoral Commission]] |date=21 September 2014}}{{cite news |last1=Mathewson |first1=Nicole |last2=Stylianou |first2=Georgina |last3=Fulton |first3=Tim |title=Election 2014: Canterbury decides |url= http://www.stuff.co.nz/the-press/news/10524525/Election-2014-Canterbury-decides |access-date=21 September 2014 |work=[[The Press]] |date=21 September 2014}} In her first term, she was a member (subsequently deputy chairperson and chairperson) of the [[Finance and Expenditure Committee]], and also chaired the Electoral Legislation Committee that considered legislation to replace the [[Electoral Finance Act 2007]]. In 2009 her Fair Trading (Soliciting on Behalf of Charities) Amendment Bill was drawn from the member's ballot.{{cite web |url=https://www.parliament.nz/en/pb/hansard-debates/rhr/document/49HansD_20091209_00000914/fair-trading-soliciting-on-behalf-of-charities-amendment |title=Fair Trading (Soliciting on Behalf of Charities) Amendment Bill – First reading|publisher=New Zealand Parliament |date=9 December 2009| access-date=13 October 2019}} The bill required fundraising companies to disclose the proportion of funds they passed on to the charities they collect for.{{cite web |url=http://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/3145108/Bill-forces-donation-disclosure |title=Bill forces donation disclosure | work=[[Stuff.co.nz]] |date=9 December 2009 |access-date=10 December 2009}} The bill passed and became the Fair Trading (Soliciting on Behalf of Charities) Amendment Act 2012.{{cite web |url=http://www.legislation.govt.nz/act/public/2012/0048/latest/whole.html|title=Fair Trading (Soliciting on Behalf of Charities) Amendment Act 2012|publisher=New Zealand Government|access-date=13 October 2019}} Adams was made Chairperson of the Finance and Expenditure Committee and the Electoral Legislation Committee for the final months of the 49th Parliament. When the National-led government won a second term in 2011, she was appointed to the Cabinet as [[Minister of Internal Affairs (New Zealand)|Minister of Internal Affairs]], Minister for Communications and Information Technology, and Associate Minister for Canterbury Earthquake Recovery. After a reshuffle of cabinet responsibilities caused by the resignation of [[Nick Smith (New Zealand politician)|Nick Smith]], Adams was made [[Minister for the Environment (New Zealand)|Minister for the Environment]]. [[Chris Tremain]] succeeded her in the Internal Affairs portfolio. After National won the [[2014 New Zealand general election|2014 general election]] in September, Adams became the [[Minister of Justice (New Zealand)|Minister of Justice]], [[Minister for Courts]], [[Minister of Broadcasting (New Zealand)|Minister of Broadcasting]] and [[Minister of Communications (New Zealand)|Minister of Communications]]. As Minister of Justice, she wiped the convictions of men convicted of homosexual acts prior to the [[Homosexual Law Reform Act 1986|decriminalisation of homosexuality in 1986]], and apologised on behalf of the government.{{Cite news |title=Watch: The moment Amy Adams apologises on behalf of Government for convicting gay men for homosexual acts prior to 1986 |url=https://www.tvnz.co.nz/one-news/new-zealand/watch-moment-amy-adams-apologises-behalf-government-convicting-gay-men-homosexual-acts-prior-1986 |access-date=2020-11-14 |work=TVNZ |language=en-NZ}} Following [[Bill English]]'s elevation to [[Prime Minister of New Zealand|Prime Minister]] in 2016, Adams also took on the roles of [[Minister for Social Housing]], Minister Responsible for Social Investment, Minister Responsible for [[Housing New Zealand]] and [[Associate Minister of Finance (New Zealand)|Associate Minister of Finance]], in addition to retaining the justice and courts portfolios.{{Cite news|title=Adams, Amy|language=en|url=https://www.parliament.nz/en/mps-and-electorates/former-members-of-parliament/adams-amy/|access-date=2020-11-14}} ===Opposition, 2017–2020=== Following the formation of a [[Sixth Labour Government of New Zealand|Labour-led coalition government]] after the [[2017 New Zealand general election|2017 general election]], English resigned as party leader and Adams contested the [[2018 New Zealand National Party leadership election|subsequent leadership election]].{{cite web|title=Amy Adams announces bid for National leadership|url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=11994380|work=[[The New Zealand Herald]]|date=14 February 2018|author=Chang, Derek}} [[Simon Bridges]] was elected, with Adams considered the next closest contestant.{{cite news |url=https://www.odt.co.nz/news/national/amy-adams-replaces-joyce-nationals-finance-role |title=Amy Adams replaces Joyce in National's finance role |work=[[Otago Daily Times]] |date=7 March 2018 |access-date=14 July 2020}} She became National's finance spokesperson in [[Shadow Cabinet of Simon Bridges|Bridges' Shadow Cabinet]], ranked third in the caucus and served on the [[Finance and Expenditure Committee|Finance and Expenditure]] and Privileges select committees.{{cite web |title=Hon Amy Adams |url=https://www.parliament.nz/en/mps-and-electorates/members-of-parliament/adams-amy/ |website=[[New Zealand Parliament]] |access-date=23 January 2019}} On 22 January 2019, Adams was designated as the shadow [[Attorney-General (New Zealand)|Attorney-General]] following the retirement of [[Chris Finlayson]].{{cite news |title=Bennett named drug reform spokesperson in shadow cabinet reshuffle |url=https://www.radionz.co.nz/news/national/380645/bennett-named-drug-reform-spokesperson-in-shadow-cabinet-reshuffle |access-date=23 January 2019 |work=[[Radio New Zealand]] |date=22 January 2019}}{{cite news |last1=Coughlan |first1=Thomas |title=Bridges begins year with a reshuffle |url=https://www.newsroom.co.nz/2019/01/22/409336/bridges-begins-year-with-a-reshuffle |access-date=23 January 2019 | work=[[Newsroom (website)|Newsroom]] |date=22 January 2019}} In June 2019, Adams announced that she would retire from politics at the [[2020 New Zealand general election|2020 general election]], and that she would step down from her party spokesperson roles immediately.{{cite news |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=12243700 |title=National's Amy Adams retiring from politics at 2020 election |date=25 June 2019 |work=New Zealand Herald |access-date=25 June 2019}} She was replaced as National's candidate in Selwyn by journalist [[Nicola Grigg]]. While a backbencher, Adams was appointed deputy chair of the committee that considered the [[Abortion Legislation Act 2020|Abortion Legislation Bill]]. After [[Todd Muller]] replaced Bridges as National Party leader in a [[May 2020 New Zealand National Party leadership election|leadership challenge in May 2020]], Adams rescinded her retirement and was given the party's [[COVID-19 pandemic in New Zealand|COVID-19 Recovery]] portfolio and a ranking of 3 in [[Shadow Cabinet of Todd Muller|Muller's Shadow Cabinet]].{{Cite news |title=National == Later career == On 23 September 2021, [[Sixth Labour Government of New Zealand|Labour]] [[Minister of Health (New Zealand)|Health Minister]] [[Andrew Little (New Zealand politician)|Andrew Little]] announced that Adams would be among the first people appointed to the board of [[Health New Zealand]], the new health authority being established to replace New Zealand's [[district health board]]s.{{Cite news |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/health/126467568/health-new-zealand-and-mori-health-authority-board-members-announced|title=Health New Zealand and Māori Health Authority board members announced|date=22 September 2021|work =Stuff}} Adams began studying pre-hospital emergency care and is a volunteer ambulance officer.{{cite news |last=Jacobson |first=Julie |date=27 January 2024 |title=Life after politics: Finding a new buzz beyond the Beehive |url=https://www.thepost.co.nz/nz-news/350156526/life-after-politics-finding-new-buzz-beyond-beehive |accessdate=27 January 2024 |work=[[The Post (New Zealand newspaper)|The Post]]}} In September 2021, Adams began a four-year term on the [[University of Canterbury]] governing council. She became [[Chancellor (education)|chancellor]] of the university in March 2022 and was reappointed for a second term on the council in September 2025.{{cite web |date=2 March 2022 |title=New Chancellor Amy Adams appointed at the University of Canterbury |url=https://www.canterbury.ac.nz/news-and-events/news/new-chancellor-amy-adams-appointed-at-the-university-of-canterbu |url-status=live
